query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys, thermally activated super‐jogging of edge dislocations limits their mobility at elevated temperatures. This mechanism retards dislocation glide, which in turn produces a plateau in yield strength and a near temperature–independent elastic (thermoelastic) response.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase BCC refractory high–entropy alloy (for example, NbTaHfTiZrV0.5) prepared via standard melting and prolonged high‐temperature homogenization to eliminate segregation.
generation.intervention: Introduce an annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (distinct from the service temperature) designed to promote recovery and reduce the density/pinning of edge dislocations relative to the as‐processed baseline. This slight microstructural modification is expected to modify the edge dislocation network.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing by nanoindentation creep under a constant high load (>1 N) in high vacuum, performed at controlled elevated temperatures (approximately 673–1073 K). Testing is conducted under static constant load hold conditions so that the dislocation–mediated deformation (and any thermal effects) can be monitored.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and spatial distribution of edge dislocations.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, edge dislocations experience thermal super‐jogging that effectively retards their glide. This impedes plastic deformation and results in a strength plateau and minimal degradation of elastic moduli. Reducing the pinning and perhaps the density of these dislocations (via a controlled annealing treatment) should enhance their mobility and thereby alter the observed high–temperature mechanical and thermoelastic responses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as–processed HEA, the annealed (recovered) sample is predicted to exhibit a weakened high–temperature yield strength plateau and a stronger temperature dependence of both yield strength and elastic modulus, indicating enhanced motion of edge dislocations.
generation.baseline: The as–processed, homogenized refractory HEA possessing a high density of pinned edge dislocations that underlies the observed high–temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior.
generation.boundary: Tests are conducted under high vacuum to preclude oxidation, at service–relevant elevated temperatures (673–1073 K) and at high load (above 1 N) using static constant load hold nanoindentation, ensuring that the stress state is similar to that in intended high–temperature applications.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the yield strength reduction and change in temperature sensitivity is uncertain due to limited prior quantitative data; thus, the intervention’s effects may require further optimization to clearly delineate the role of edge dislocation super–jogging.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 HEA specimens: one in the standard as–processed (homogenized) state and one subjected to the intermediate annealing treatment aimed at reducing the density or effective pinning of edge dislocations. Subject both sets to nanoindentation creep experiments across a temperature range of 673–1073 K under a constant, high load (>1 N) in high vacuum.
measurements: Yield strength as a function of temperature
Elastic modulus (thermoelastic response) derived from nanoindentation data
Creep displacement rates and evaluation of creep stress exponents
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the yield strength plateau or an increased temperature sensitivity of the elastic modulus and yield strength (i.e. if their mechanical responses remain indistinguishable from the baseline as–processed samples), then the hypothesis that edge dislocation super–jogging is the governing mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations.
